chapter: Return to Chicago: the Blue Note and Rupneck's
title: Returning to Chicago in 1949: Pee Wee and Art's Back Room
summary: Hodes goes back to 1949 and the Back Room, where Phil Harris, Teagarden, Lips Page and Red Allen came. He lists his children and says he stopped drinking.

venues.name: Pee Wee and Art's Back Room

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: So when did you come back to Chicago? And what were the circumstances? What had been happening in Chicago from what we'd been talking about earlier?
Okay, now we go back to 1949. Pee Wee and Art have opened up Pee Wee and Art's Back Room. Phil Harris is coming in on a Friday night and fooling with the forks. He's a drummer.

Yes. And we're beginning to attract people. Eddie Condon gives us a show on television, Pee Wee and Art's Back Room, gives us George Wattley gives us, like, a quick two-number shot. Well, we're getting known, and the joint is beginning to fill up. We're getting a $30 a week draw, $35. Pee Wee never got too much because I stopped drinking then, and Pee Wee didn't. So Pee Wee's money always went for the booze, and my money was going to support the family. And we'd moved out of the town a little bit. We had some children. It's a good thing I stopped.
At that time, we had three and one was on the way. We had six children, but five lived. I lost one, that was a tragedy, one of the tragedies we had. But -- 19 months old.

Anyway, so I was getting a little more money all the time. So I was getting a little more money all the time. I wound up getting $110 a week before I left. And during that time, like I say, we booked Jack Teagarden and his whole band, in which we had a new clarinet player every night, even if we had to send to Philadelphia for him. And we had Lips Paige came in every Friday religiously, if he wasn't working in Blue. Red Allen came in, for free.

And they all supported us. The drinks were very nominal. It wasn't a big deal, it was a very small room. 90 people in that room, you had to sit in one another's laps. And Pee Wee would sit at any table. I told Pee Wee, now, don't worry about it, don't even think about it. When I go up there with Herb, wherever you're sitting is good. But --
With Herb Ward, the bass player. But do carry your clarinet, so if you feel like blowing, start blowing from the table. It sounded good, looked good.
And that's what we did. And then we got Willie the Lion Smith, we grew in stature. We got Chippy Hill, we got Willie. It got to be a place to go.
